speaker_role: independent counselor (college admissions consultant, also a college student)
commercial_incentive: Promotes a free downloadable spreadsheet template; mentions working for an unnamed 'big international' admissions consulting firm
key_insights: Frames the activities list as providing evidence for the applicant's overall narrative/story and as a signal of likely future achievement based on past accomplishments.
States admissions readers spend only a few minutes scanning an activities list, so entries must be quick and memorable.
Offers a writing formula: summarize each activity into three points (accomplishment, impact, outcome) combined into one semicolon-separated sentence to maximize the character limit.
Recommends quantifying impact wherever possible (numbers served, percent growth, membership increases) rather than vague claims.
Suggests three possible ways to order the list: by importance/impressiveness, chronologically, or grouped by theme (her preferred method).
Recommends using the Common App 'additional information' section to expand on top activities or include strong activities that didn't make the top 10 list.
States family caregiving obligations (e.g., caring for a sick relative) count as legitimate extracurricular activities and can add context that makes other accomplishments more impressive.
Advises using a separate spreadsheet to draft and track activities (with character counts and themes) before transferring to the Common App.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker: Common App activities section allows 10 activities, 50 characters for position/organization, 150 characters for description
Speaker (personal anecdote): described her own admission to Yale-NUS with a cited ~4.5% admit rate the year she applied
notable_or_distinctive: Gives a concrete, reusable 'accomplishment; impact; outcome' semicolon-separated writing template with worked examples from the speaker's own real activities list.
reliability_notes: Advice is the speaker's personal method as a college student/junior consultant, not sourced from official admissions data; her own 4.5% admit-rate claim is self-reported and unverified.
